newsitem.title: USA: White House, Congress wrapping up budget issues.
newsitem.headline: White House, Congress wrapping up budget issues.

text.p: White House officials and Republican lawmakers struggled Wednesday to work out differences on the budget that threatened to delay $5.5 billion in disaster relief.

While negotiations continued, the Senate debated the disaster relief bill and approved an amendment to extend supplemental income benefits for elderly and disabled legal immigrants for another two months, through Sept. 30, at a cost of $240 million. Benefits for this group were to end Aug. 22.

President Clinton has threatened to veto the disaster relief bill if it arrives on his desk with a Republican-crafted provision designed to prevent future government shutdowns. The Republican plan would automatically continue federal spending at a 98 percent level after Oct. 1 even if regular spending bills have not been enacted.
Such disputes forced two government shutdowns in 1996 which polls showed the public blamed on Republicans.
The House held off votes on its version until next week.

The disaster relief bill also would provide nearly $2 billion to pay for U.S. military operations in Bosnia and the Gulf. The White House also objected to the proposed waiver of environmental laws for flood control projects.
At the same time, the White House and lawmakers disputed the details of a just-concluded agreement to balance the budget over the next five years.

Republicans said they had not agreed to a specific $35 billion in tax relief for Clinton's education initiatives as part of the gross $135 billion in tax cuts over five years. Democrats said this was part of the budget deal.
Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott said the education tax credits were not on his party's list of priorities -- a capital gains tax rate cut, a $500 per child tax credit and lower inheritance taxes.
"We can't have too large a chunk of revenue changes go into that one area," Lott said when asked if the $35 billion tax credit for education was assured in the budget deal.
"We will have to have room for a capital gains tax rate cut to around 20 percent and the tax credit for families to $500," the Mississippi Republican said.
Still, White House congressional liaison John Hilley told reporters he understood that "the vast part of the tax bill will be going toward education and the child credit."

The budget agreement would bring the government deficit to zero by 2002, enact the tax cut package, trim Medicare health care spending by $115 billion and pay for some of the president's domestic priorities.
Senate Democratic Leader Tom Daschle said he expected a vast majority of his colleagues would vote for the final budget. It was expected to be before the Senate by May 23.
"By and large, well over three-fourths of our caucus will support this budget agreement," the South Dakota Democrat told reporters.

While the disaster relief funds and the budget are separate legislation, they are linked by the Republican effort to continue federal spending beyond the start of the new fiscal year at levels lower than agreed to last week.
If the automatic spending bill is passed in some form, Democrats would like to see funding assured at the levels set in the budget agreement reached last Friday.
"We have bargained in good faith to reach this, and now anything that's done automatically must be consistent with that," Daschle said.
